prompt: Which statement best distinguishes economic development from economic growth?

options.label: A
options.text: Development: nominal income; growth: real income

options.label: B
options.text: Development: industry output; growth: services output

options.label: C
options.text: Development: broader welfare; growth: higher output

options.label: D
options.text: Development: export receipts; growth: import spending

explanation: Economic growth concerns the amount of output or productive capacity. Development is wider and includes health, education, poverty, opportunity and other aspects of well-being.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.1 classification of economies in terms of their level of development | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why can two countries with similar real GDP per head be classified at different levels of development?

options.label: A
options.text: Health, education and distribution can differ

options.label: B
options.text: Average income determines every aspect of development

options.label: C
options.text: Equal average income guarantees equal human development

options.label: D
options.text: Development classifications exclude every non-monetary welfare indicator

explanation: Development is multidimensional. Similar average incomes can coexist with very different life expectancy, schooling, poverty and distributional outcomes.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.1 classification of economies in terms of their level of development | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which description is most consistent with a developed economy?

options.label: A
options.text: Low productivity and extensive subsistence production

options.label: B
options.text: Low average incomes and limited formal markets

options.label: C
options.text: All employment concentrated in primary-sector production

options.label: D
options.text: High productivity and mature, diversified markets

explanation: The coursebook associates developed economies with high GDP per head, high productivity, mature markets and relatively high living standards.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.1 classification of economies in terms of their level of development | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which description is most consistent with an emerging economy?

options.label: A
options.text: An economy in which no productive manufacturing sector has developed

options.label: B
options.text: An economy with continually declining real incomes

options.label: C
options.text: An economy poorer than every developing economy

options.label: D
options.text: Industrialisation with rising income

explanation: Emerging economies are generally undergoing rapid growth and structural transformation while remaining below the development level of advanced economies on important indicators.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.1 classification of economies in terms of their level of development | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Why is classification by national income per head alone an incomplete measure of development?

options.label: A
options.text: Averages omit distribution and wider welfare outcomes

options.label: B
options.text: Income statistics include every unpaid household activity

options.label: C
options.text: Income statistics are measured only in physical units

options.label: D
options.text: Higher average incomes necessarily reduce life expectancy

explanation: Income is useful but it is an average monetary measure. Development also depends on factors such as health, education, distribution and environmental quality.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.2 classification of economies in terms of their level of national income | 11.3.3 indicators | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A classification system states that economies with GNI per head below $1 500 are low income, $1 500-$12 000 are middle income and above $12 000 are high income. How would a country with GNI per head of $8 400 be classified?

options.label: A
options.text: Low income

options.label: B
options.text: High income

options.label: C
options.text: Very high human development

options.label: D
options.text: Middle income

explanation: The stated thresholds place $8 400 within the middle-income band. This is an income classification, not an HDI classification.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.2 classification of economies in terms of their level of national income | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What is real GDP per head?

options.label: A
options.text: Real GDP / population

options.label: B
options.text: Nominal GDP / price index

options.label: C
options.text: Real GDP × population

options.label: D
options.text: Gross national income − depreciation

explanation: Real GDP per head adjusts output for inflation and then expresses it as an average per person.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 monetary indicators: real per capita national income statistics | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What adjustment converts GNI into NNI?

options.label: A
options.text: Add depreciation

options.label: B
options.text: Subtract foreign income

options.label: C
options.text: Add indirect taxes

options.label: D
options.text: Subtract depreciation

explanation: NNI measures national income after allowing for the consumption of fixed capital, so depreciation is deducted from GNI.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 monetary indicators: GDP, GNI and NNI | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Country X has GDP of $420bn, net income from abroad of +$18bn and depreciation of $28bn. What is its NNI?
explanation: GNI = GDP + net income from abroad = 438. NNI = GNI - depreciation = 438 - 28 = $410bn.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 monetary indicators: GDP, GNI and NNI | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why is purchasing power parity useful when comparing living standards between countries?

options.label: A
options.text: It fixes every country’s nominal currency quote

options.label: B
options.text: It removes inequality between households within countries

options.label: C
options.text: It measures only relative quantities of export goods

options.label: D
options.text: It adjusts for differences in domestic price levels

explanation: Market exchange rates do not necessarily reflect what incomes can buy locally. PPP comparisons attempt to compare purchasing power more directly.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 purchasing power parity | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: If identical baskets of goods are much cheaper in country A than country B, what is most likely when market-exchange-rate incomes are converted using PPP?

options.label: A
options.text: A’s relative purchasing power is revised upward

options.label: B
options.text: A’s relative purchasing power is revised downward

options.label: C
options.text: A and B necessarily have identical living standards

options.label: D
options.text: A and B cannot be compared using PPP

explanation: When prices are lower in A, a given income buys more goods and services there, so PPP conversion tends to raise A relative to a simple market-rate comparison.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 purchasing power parity | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which is a non-monetary indicator of living standards?

options.label: A
options.text: Real GNI per head

options.label: B
options.text: Infant mortality rate

options.label: C
options.text: Real GDP per head

options.label: D
options.text: Real NNI per head

explanation: Infant mortality is measured in physical demographic terms rather than money values and can reveal health and welfare conditions.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 non-monetary indicators | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which is most likely to indicate higher living standards?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher infant mortality

options.label: B
options.text: Higher life expectancy

options.label: C
options.text: Lower literacy

options.label: D
options.text: Lower access to safe water

explanation: Longer life expectancy is generally associated with better health, nutrition, sanitation and access to medical care.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 non-monetary indicators | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which three broad dimensions are included in the Human Development Index?

options.label: A
options.text: Inflation, unemployment and trade

options.label: B
options.text: Income, education and health

options.label: C
options.text: Taxation, government debt and interest rates

options.label: D
options.text: Exports, imports and exchange rates

explanation: HDI combines GNI per head with education and life expectancy, reflecting income, knowledge and health.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 composite indicators: Human Development Index | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which variable is used in the health dimension of the HDI?

options.label: A
options.text: Life expectancy

options.label: B
options.text: Unemployment rate

options.label: C
options.text: Consumer price inflation

options.label: D
options.text: Birth rate alone

explanation: Life expectancy is the health measure used in the HDI.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 composite indicators: Human Development Index | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which variable is used in the income dimension of the HDI?

options.label: A
options.text: PPP-adjusted GNI per head

options.label: B
options.text: Total nominal GDP at market prices

options.label: C
options.text: Government expenditure per head

options.label: D
options.text: The income distribution’s Gini coefficient

explanation: The HDI uses GNI per head as its income component rather than total national output.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 composite indicators: Human Development Index | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: What does the Measure of Economic Welfare attempt to do?

options.label: A
options.text: Adjust output measures for wider welfare costs and benefits

options.label: B
options.text: Replace output measures with the unemployed share of workers

options.label: C
options.text: Count only marketed goods and exclude non-market welfare effects

options.label: D
options.text: Count only income shares and exclude production’s welfare effects

explanation: MEW modifies GDP by allowing for welfare-relevant items that GDP does not capture well, such as leisure and some negative effects of production.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 composite indicators: Measure of Economic Welfare | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which change would tend to increase MEW relative to GDP?

options.label: A
options.text: More pollution with unchanged output

options.label: B
options.text: More leisure with essential consumption unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: Longer commuting with unchanged output

options.label: D
options.text: A higher incidence of crime without any change in aggregate economic production

explanation: MEW adds or recognises welfare-enhancing factors such as leisure and deducts welfare-reducing factors.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 composite indicators: Measure of Economic Welfare | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which is included in the Multidimensional Poverty Index?

options.label: A
options.text: Safe drinking-water access

options.label: B
options.text: The policy interest rate

options.label: C
options.text: The nominal exchange rate

options.label: D
options.text: The government budget balance

explanation: The MPI combines deprivations in living standards, education and health, including access to safe water.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 composite indicators: Multidimensional Poverty Index | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: A household is deprived in at least one third of the weighted global MPI indicators. How is it classified?

options.label: A
options.text: High-income household

options.label: B
options.text: Multidimensionally poor household

options.label: C
options.text: Fully developed household

options.label: D
options.text: Income-only poor household

explanation: Under the global Multidimensional Poverty Index, a household is multidimensionally poor when its weighted deprivation score is at least one third. The threshold includes exactly one third, not only scores above it.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 composite indicators: Multidimensional Poverty Index | AO2 Analysis

prompt: What shape is the Kuznets curve?

options.label: A
options.text: A vertical line

options.label: B
options.text: An inverted U

options.label: C
options.text: A downward-sloping straight line

options.label: D
options.text: A J-shape

explanation: The Kuznets hypothesis suggests inequality first rises and later falls as economic development proceeds, creating an inverted-U relationship.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 the Kuznets curve | AO1 Knowledge and understanding
graphDescription: Vertical axis: income inequality. Horizontal axis: income per head or level of economic development. Draw an inverted-U curve labelled Kuznets curve, with inequality rising at low-to-middle development levels and falling at higher levels.

graphScenes.caption: Schematic; labeled numbers specify quantitative values.

prompt: According to the Kuznets hypothesis, what may happen to income inequality in the early stages of development?

options.label: A
options.text: Income inequality immediately disappears

options.label: B
options.text: Inequality has no relationship with changes in the economy’s productive structure

options.label: C
options.text: Income inequality necessarily remains unchanged

options.label: D
options.text: Inequality can rise with early industrialisation

explanation: The initial development process can widen income differences as some workers enter higher-productivity sectors before the rest of the economy catches up.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 the Kuznets curve | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country's real GDP grows by 5% while its population grows by 2%. What happens approximately to real GDP per head?

options.label: A
options.text: It rises by about 7%

options.label: B
options.text: It rises by about 3%

options.label: C
options.text: It falls by about 3%

options.label: D
options.text: It is unchanged

explanation: Per-capita growth is approximately real GDP growth minus population growth, so about 5% - 2% = 3%.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.4 comparison of economic growth rates and living standards over time | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why can a high economic growth rate fail to raise average living standards?

options.label: A
options.text: Output growth necessarily reduces income per head

options.label: B
options.text: Population growth can offset output growth

options.label: C
options.text: Output has no relationship with living standards

options.label: D
options.text: Output growth necessarily reduces household consumption

explanation: Total output can rise while output per person does not. Per-capita measures are therefore important when linking growth to living standards.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.4 comparison of economic growth rates and living standards | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Country A has real GDP per head of $50 000 and grows by 2%. Country B has $5 000 and grows by 8%. Which statement is correct after one year?

options.label: A
options.text: B exceeds A’s output per head immediately

options.label: B
options.text: A retains higher output per head

options.label: C
options.text: A and B have identical output per head

options.label: D
options.text: Both countries’ output per head remains unchanged

explanation: Growth rates describe percentage changes, not starting levels. A high growth rate from a low base can coexist with a much lower income level.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.4 comparison over time and between countries | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why should real rather than nominal income per head be used to compare living standards over time?

options.label: A
options.text: It removes the effect of price changes

options.label: B
options.text: It includes every change in nominal prices

options.label: C
options.text: It excludes the value of productive output

options.label: D
options.text: It necessarily remains below nominal income

explanation: A nominal rise may simply reflect inflation. Real measures are needed to identify changes in purchasing power and output.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 monetary indicators | 11.3.4 comparison over time | AO1 Knowledge and understanding

prompt: Which problem can make GDP per head overstate an improvement in living standards?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher defensive spending following crime or pollution

options.label: B
options.text: Additional consumer production with no accompanying rise in pollution or criminal activity

options.label: C
options.text: Longer life expectancy without additional defensive spending

options.label: D
options.text: Better school attendance without additional defensive spending

explanation: GDP records production expenditure but does not automatically distinguish activity that directly improves welfare from defensive expenditure.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 issues of comparison using monetary indicators | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which problem can make official GDP understate living standards in an economy?

options.label: A
options.text: Output is counted twice in national statistics

options.label: B
options.text: All market prices are legally fixed

options.label: C
options.text: Every household activity has a recorded market value

options.label: D
options.text: Useful non-market household production remains unrecorded

explanation: Non-marketed household and voluntary production may create welfare but is not fully included in official market-based GDP.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 issues of comparison using monetary indicators | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country's HDI rises while real GDP per head is unchanged. What can explain this?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher GDP alone determines all HDI dimensions

options.label: B
options.text: Higher inflation directly improves all HDI dimensions

options.label: C
options.text: Lower population automatically raises all HDI dimensions

options.label: D
options.text: Better health and education raise non-income dimensions

explanation: HDI is multidimensional, so improved life expectancy or schooling can raise the index even without higher real GDP per head.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 HDI | 11.3.4 living standards over time | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which statement about economic growth and development is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: An increase in total output necessarily delivers improved living standards for every household

options.label: B
options.text: Nominal GDP alone measures every aspect of development

options.label: C
options.text: Output supports development; distribution and welfare also matter

options.label: D
options.text: Environmental welfare has no relationship with broader development

explanation: Higher output can create resources for better living standards, but development is not automatic and depends on distribution, public services and broader welfare.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.1 classification by development | 11.3.4 growth and living standards | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Country X has high GNI per head but low life expectancy and weak schooling outcomes. Which classification problem does this illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: High income necessarily implies an even higher HDI ranking

options.label: B
options.text: Income rankings can exceed broader human-development rankings

options.label: C
options.text: High income guarantees equally strong schooling and health outcomes

options.label: D
options.text: Life expectancy belongs to development’s monetary-income dimension

explanation: Income per head captures command over goods and services but can miss weak health and education outcomes. A multidimensional measure may rank X lower.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.1 level of development | 11.3.2 national income | 11.3.3 HDI | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Country A is classified as high income but has severe inequality and extensive multidimensional poverty. What is the best conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: High average income can coexist with serious deprivation

options.label: B
options.text: High average income cannot coexist with any poor households

options.label: C
options.text: High average income guarantees every household meets every basic need

options.label: D
options.text: Income classification and multidimensional deprivation measure identical outcomes

explanation: A high average income can coexist with poor distribution and deprivation in health, education and living standards.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.1-11.3.3 classification and indicators | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A country has GDP of $900bn, net income from abroad of -$40bn, depreciation of $60bn and population of 100m. What is NNI per head?
explanation: GNI = 900 - 40 = 860bn. NNI = 860 - 60 = 800bn. Dividing by 100m gives $8 000 per head.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 monetary indicators: real per capita national income statistics | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country's nominal GDP per head rises 12% while its price level rises 9%. What is the approximate rise in real GDP per head?

options.label: A
options.text: About 21%

options.label: B
options.text: About 3%

options.label: C
options.text: About 12%

options.label: D
options.text: About 9%

explanation: For an approximate comparison, real growth is nominal growth minus inflation: 12% - 9% = about 3%.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 real per capita national income | 11.3.4 comparison over time | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Country A has market-exchange-rate income per head of $10 000 and a local price level half that of the reference country. What is the main purpose of a PPP adjustment?

options.label: A
options.text: Fix the nominal currency exchange rate

options.label: B
options.text: Eliminate income inequality within the country

options.label: C
options.text: Adjust income for cheaper local goods

options.label: D
options.text: Deduct depreciation from gross national income

explanation: PPP attempts to compare what incomes can actually purchase rather than relying only on currency-market conversion.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 purchasing power parity | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why can using market exchange rates give a misleading comparison of living standards?

options.label: A
options.text: The market exchange rate always provides the same conversion as purchasing-power-parity adjustments

options.label: B
options.text: Market exchange rates cannot change between different years

options.label: C
options.text: Market exchange rates directly measure life expectancy outcomes

options.label: D
options.text: Capital flows can move rates independently of prices

explanation: Currency values reflect many factors besides the prices of everyday goods and services. PPP is designed to address this problem.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 issues of comparison using monetary indicators | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A country has a very large informal sector that is not recorded. How is official GDP per head most likely affected?

options.label: A
options.text: Recorded income necessarily exceeds actual production

options.label: B
options.text: Recorded GDP becomes identical to residents’ GNI

options.label: C
options.text: Recorded income no longer requires PPP adjustment

options.label: D
options.text: Recorded income excludes useful unrecorded production

explanation: Unrecorded market or near-market activity contributes to actual production but may be absent from official national-income data.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 issues of comparison using monetary indicators | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why can a change in the size of the shadow economy distort comparisons of economic growth over time?

options.label: A
options.text: All output generated by unrecorded activities is already included in official GDP estimates

options.label: B
options.text: Measured growth is independent of statistical coverage

options.label: C
options.text: Coverage changes may differ from production changes

options.label: D
options.text: Unrecorded production influences prices but never measured output

explanation: If more or less activity moves into the recorded sector, official growth can differ from the change in total economic activity.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 monetary comparison issues | 11.3.4 growth over time | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Country X reports faster real GDP growth than country Y, but X is rapidly depleting non-renewable resources. What additional issue matters when comparing development?

options.label: A
options.text: The bilateral nominal exchange rate alone

options.label: B
options.text: The domestic money supply growth rate alone

options.label: C
options.text: The sustainability and welfare consequences of production

options.label: D
options.text: The annual balance on the current account alone

prompt: Real GDP per head rises by 6%, but the Gini coefficient rises sharply and median household income is unchanged. What is the strongest conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: Average income rises without equal gains for typical households

options.label: C
options.text: Every household necessarily becomes poorer despite higher average income

options.label: D
options.text: Income distribution cannot influence any assessment of economic development

reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 issues of comparison using monetary indicators | 11.3.4 living standards | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which pair of changes would most unambiguously suggest an improvement in development?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher inflation and higher fiscal borrowing

options.label: B
options.text: Higher nominal output but faster price growth

options.label: C
options.text: Higher population with unchanged real national output

options.label: D
options.text: Lower infant mortality and higher school attendance

explanation: Health and education improvements directly indicate better non-monetary development outcomes.
reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 non-monetary indicators | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Country A has higher real GDP per head than country B, but B has lower infant mortality and higher literacy. What can be concluded?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher income guarantees A ranks first on every indicator

options.label: B
options.text: Income and social indicators can produce different country rankings

prompt: Which change would increase MEW but leave measured GDP unchanged?

options.label: A
options.text: More pollution with unchanged production

options.label: B
options.text: More leisure with unchanged production

options.label: C
options.text: Longer commuting with unchanged production

options.label: D
options.text: Higher crime with unchanged production

reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 Measure of Economic Welfare | AO2 Analysis

prompt: GDP rises because households spend more on cleaning up pollution caused by production. How would MEW most likely treat this compared with GDP?

options.label: A

options.text: Pollution’s welfare costs qualify the measured output increase

options.label: C
options.text: GDP and welfare measures must always move identically together

prompt: Why is MEW difficult to calculate precisely?

options.label: A

options.text: Every component already has an observable market price

options.text: GDP cannot be measured using any monetary values

options.label: D
options.text: MEW includes only directly observed physical output quantities

prompt: Why might inequality eventually fall as development proceeds according to Kuznets reasoning?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: A return of all workers to agriculture

options.label: C
options.text: Legislation making every household income identical

options.label: D

prompt: Country X grows at 4% annually for five years while population grows at 1% annually. Country Y grows at 3% while population is unchanged. Which has the faster approximate growth of real GDP per head?

options.label: D

prompt: Country A starts with real GDP per head of $40 000 and grows 1%. Country B starts at $4 000 and grows 6%. Why is it misleading to say B has the higher living standard?

options.label: B

options.label: C

prompt: What makes comparisons of real GDP per head between countries difficult even after adjusting for inflation?

options.label: A

prompt: A low-income country has 8% real GDP growth but 7% population growth. A high-income country has 2.5% real GDP growth and 0.5% population growth. Which has the larger approximate rise in real GDP per head?

prompt: A country's real GDP per head rises, life expectancy falls and pollution rises. What is the best judgement?

prompt: A government increases free education and healthcare. GDP rises only slightly. Why can development still improve significantly?

prompt: Country X has real GDP per head twice that of Y at market exchange rates, but only 1.3 times Y at PPP. What does this suggest?

prompt: Why is a high HDI not sufficient to prove that income is equally distributed?

options.label: C

options.text: HDI can be calculated only for low-income countries

prompt: A country's nominal GNI per head rises 10%, the domestic price level rises 6%, and its population is unchanged. What is the approximate change in real GNI per head?

prompt: GDP is $700bn, net income from abroad is +$50bn, depreciation is $30bn and population is 80m. Which per-capita measure is highest?

prompt: Why can a rise in real GDP caused mainly by longer working hours overstate the improvement in welfare?

prompt: Which indicator would be most useful for identifying poverty that is not captured by income alone?

prompt: Which indicator is most directly suited to comparing average command over goods and services across countries with very different price levels?

prompt: A country's HDI improves because mean years of schooling rise. Which dimension of development has improved most directly?

prompt: A country has lower GDP per head than another but higher MEW. Which explanation is plausible?

options.label: A

options.text: Exclusion of every form of non-market welfare

options.label: C

options.label: D

prompt: Which conclusion is safest when one country has a higher economic growth rate but a lower HDI than another?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.text: Indicators of human development measure only the annual rate of output expansion

options.label: D

prompt: Country A has higher real GDP per head than country B. A also has much greater inequality, lower life expectancy and lower schooling. Which judgement is most defensible?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Income alone necessarily establishes A’s higher development level

options.label: C
options.text: Income is irrelevant and therefore B necessarily ranks higher

options.label: D
options.text: These differences imply the countries have identical HDI scores

prompt: A country moves from middle-income to high-income classification after a commodity-price boom, but education and health outcomes barely change. What is the strongest criticism of the reclassification as evidence of development?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Crossing an income threshold does not establish broader progress

options.text: Health and education outcomes belong only to monetary measures

prompt: Two countries have the same real GNI per head at PPP. Country X has a larger shadow economy than Y. Which comparison problem remains?

options.label: B
options.text: Equal recorded income establishes equal living standards

options.label: C
options.text: Informal production affects only consumer-price inflation rates

options.text: Different informal sectors mean different recording gaps

reference: 11.3 Economic development | 11.3.3 issues of comparison using monetary indicators | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Country X records 7% real GDP growth, but a large share comes from reconstruction after natural disasters. What is the best welfare interpretation?

options.label: C
options.text: Reconstruction adds output while restoring previously lost assets

options.label: D

prompt: Country A has 5% real GDP growth and 4% population growth. Country B has 3% real GDP growth and 0% population growth. Over several years, which is more likely to experience faster growth in average material living standards, other things equal?

options.label: B
options.text: Both equally

options.label: C
options.text: Country B

options.label: D
options.text: Neither country

prompt: A country's real GDP per head rises 4%, but average leisure falls, pollution rises and income inequality widens. Which index is most likely to show a smaller improvement than GDP per head?
